content: Miscarriage is defined as the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before the fetus reaches viability. Uterine muscle relaxant drugs have been utilized in women at risk of miscarriage based on the belief that these medications relax the uterine muscles, thereby potentially reducing the risk of miscarriage. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of uterine muscle relaxant drugs on both the woman and her baby when used in cases of threatened miscarriage. The researchers conducted a search within the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register on September 10, 2009, to identify relevant studies. Only randomized trials were included in the analysis, while quasi-randomized trials were excluded. The participants in the included studies were women with pregnancies of less than 20 weeks' gestation who were experiencing a threatened miscarriage. The interventions studied involved the use of any uterine muscle relaxant drugs, including tocolytic and antispasmodic agents, compared to either a placebo or no drug at all. The primary outcomes assessed were miscarriage (defined as spontaneous pregnancy loss before fetal viability), fetal death (stillbirth or neonatal death), and maternal death. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the studies and extracted the relevant data. The review included only one trial, which was of poor quality and involved 170 women. This trial compared the use of a beta-agonist to a placebo. The results indicated a lower risk of intrauterine death associated with the use of the beta-agonist, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.25 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.12 to 0.51. Preterm birth was the only other outcome reported, with a relative risk of 1.67 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.63 to 4.38. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of uterine muscle relaxant drugs in women with threatened miscarriage. They recommended that any use of these drugs should be limited to the context of randomized clinical trials.
